mainTopic: Sages' merits for long life, and the holiness of a בית הכנסת even after it is ruined.
overview: This amud finishes רבי פרידא's list of merits. He never ate meat before the מתנות were separated, which the גמרא calls an extra stringency because the הלכה does not follow רבי יצחק. He also let a כהן lead ברכת המזון. The גמרא challenges this practice from רבי יוחנן and answers that it applied only to a כהן who was his equal in Torah. Several more sages then explain what earned them long life: רבי נחוניא בן הקנה, רבי נחוניא הגדול, רבי יהושע בן קרחה, and רבי זירא. Their answers include not taking honor through another's shame, forgiving others, refusing gifts, being generous with money, and never looking at a wicked person. Next, a new משנה teaches that a ruined בית הכנסת stays holy, so ordinary uses of it are forbidden. Grass growing there is left alone, so the sad sight moves people to rebuild. The גמרא then begins a ברייתא forbidding קלות ראש in a בית הכנסת, such as eating and drinking there, and the list continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Two more of רבי פרידא's careful practices
steps.stepSummary: רבי פרידא ends his list of merits with two practices: he never led ברכת המזון in front of a כהן, and he never ate from an animal whose מתנות had not been separated.
steps.simpleTranslation: And I never said the blessing (ברכת המזון) in front of a כהן, and I never ate from an animal whose priestly gifts had not been separated.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of רבי פרידא's list of good deeds that he believes earned him long life. Here he adds two more items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first item means he always let a כהן lead ברכת המזון instead of leading it himself. The second means he waited until the זרוע, לחיים, and קיבה were set aside for the כהן before eating any of the meat. The גמרא will now examine each of these, starting with the second one.

keyTerms.meaning: I blessed. Here it means leading ברכת המזון (Grace after Meals).
A priest, a descendant of אהרן.
Were separated or lifted off (set aside).
Its gifts: the foreleg, jaws, and stomach given to the כהן from a slaughtered animal.

phrases.english: And I never recited the blessing in front of a priest,
phrases.notes: Meaning: I never led ברכת המזון while a כהן was present; I let him lead.

phrases.english: and I never ate from an animal
whose priestly gifts had not been separated.
phrases.notes: The gifts are the foreleg, jaws, and stomach (דברים יח:ג).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא בֵּרַכְתִּי לִפְנֵי כֹהֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רבי פרידא's list of merits from the previous section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי פרידא was careful to let a כהן lead ברכת המזון and never to eat meat before the מתנות were separated.

steps.title: The source for not eating before the gifts are separated
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the meat practice. רבי יצחק, in the name of רבי יוחנן, says it is forbidden to eat from such an animal. רבי יצחק adds that doing so is like eating טבל.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי יצחק said in the name of רבי יוחנן: it is forbidden to eat from an animal whose gifts have not been separated. And רבי יצחק also said: anyone who eats from such an animal is as if he is eating untithed produce (טבל).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind רבי פרידא's practice of not eating meat before the מתנות were separated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יצחק compares meat with unseparated מתנות to טבל, which is produce that still has תרומה and מעשר mixed into it. The idea is that the כהן's portion is still "inside" the animal, so eating it is like eating something that is not fully yours yet. This makes רבי פרידא's behavior sound like a real obligation, not just extra piety.

keyTerms.meaning: טבל: produce from which תרומה and מעשר have not yet been separated, which is forbidden to eat.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: As Rabbi Yitzchak said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is forbidden to eat from an animal
whose priestly gifts have not been separated.
And Rabbi Yitzchak said:
Anyone who eats from an animal
whose priestly gifts have not been separated
is as if he is eating untithed produce.
phrases.notes: טבל is produce whose תרומה and מעשר have not been removed.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source behind the second practice in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יצחק and רבי יוחנן, it is forbidden to eat meat before the מתנות are separated, and doing so is compared to eating טבל.

steps.title: The הלכה does not follow this view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that the הלכה is not like רבי יצחק. Eating before the מתנות are separated is permitted, so רבי פרידא was being extra strict.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is not in accordance with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a practical ruling: the strict view we just heard is not the accepted הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the הלכה rejects רבי יצחק's view, eating such meat is actually permitted. That is exactly why רבי פרידא could count his behavior as a special merit. He was going beyond what the law requires.

keyTerms.meaning: And the הלכה is not like him (his view is not accepted in practice).

steps.confusionAlert: Do not conclude that eating before the מתנות are separated is forbidden. The גמרא explicitly rules against that view. רבי פרידא's practice was an extra stringency.
steps.whyThisMatters: This tells us the practical הלכה: the meat is permitted. It also explains why רבי פרידא's carefulness counts as a personal merit and not just ordinary obedience.

phrases.english: And the halacha is not in accordance with him.
phrases.notes: So in practice it is permitted to eat the meat, and רבי פרידא was being stringent.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵית הִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the final ruling on the view quoted in step 2.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה permits eating meat before the מתנות are separated. רבי פרידא's practice was an extra stringency.

steps.title: Returning to the practice of letting a כהן lead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-quotes the first practice, "I never led the blessing in front of a כהן," so it can examine it.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And I never said the blessing in front of a כהן."
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. The גמרא is going back to the first practice from step 1 so it can challenge it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having finished with the meat practice, the גמרא now turns to the first item on the list. Repeating the words marks this as the new topic.

keyTerms.meaning: In front of, in the presence of.

phrases.english: "And I never recited the blessing in front of a priest"
phrases.notes: The גמרא quotes the words again in order to examine them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא בֵּרַכְתִּי לִפְנֵי כֹהֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the first practice in step 1 after finishing the second.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: This sets up an examination of רבי פרידא's practice of letting a כהן lead ברכת המזון.

steps.title: Letting someone else lead seems to be a serious offense
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the idea that this is a virtue. רבי יוחנן said that a תלמיד חכם who lets even an ignorant כהן גדול lead the blessing deserves death, because he lowers the honor of Torah.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this to say that it is a virtue? But didn't רבי יוחנן say: any תלמיד חכם who lets someone else lead the blessing in front of him, even a כהן גדול who is an עם הארץ, that תלמיד חכם deserves death. As it says, "All those who hate Me love death." Do not read it as "those who hate Me" (מְשַׂנְאַי), but as "those who make Me hated" (מַשְׂנִיאַי).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי פרידא's practice. It quotes רבי יוחנן to show that giving up the honor of leading looks like a sin, not a merit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תלמיד חכם represents the honor of Torah and of ה׳. If he gives up his honor even to a כהן גדול who is ignorant, he causes Torah, and through it ה׳, to be disrespected. That is the reading "those who make Me hated." So how could רבי פרידא list this as a reason for his long life? The answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Is this to say? This phrase introduces a challenge to an assumption.
An ignorant person, unlearned in Torah.
Deserving of death (here, at the hands of Heaven).
Do not read. Re-reading a פסוק's vowels to draw out a lesson.

steps.confusionAlert: The scholar is not the one leading the blessing. He is letting someone else lead in front of him (שֶׁמְּבָרֵךְ לְפָנָיו). The problem is that he gives up his honor.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key principle: the honor of a תלמיד חכם comes before the honor of an unlearned כהן. The resolution next will have to fit רבי פרידא's practice into this principle.

phrases.english: Is this to say that it is a virtue?
But didn't Rabbi Yochanan say:
Any Torah scholar in front of whom someone else leads the blessing,
even if that person is a High Priest who is an ignoramus —
that Torah scholar deserves death,
phrases.notes: Because he belittles the honor of Torah.

phrases.english: as it is stated: "All those who hate Me love death" (Mishlei 8:36).
Do not read it as "those who hate Me,"
but rather as "those who make Me hated."
phrases.notes: By lowering the honor of Torah, he causes others to disrespect God.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דִּמְעַלְּיוּתָא הִיא? וְהָא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the practice that was re-quoted in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי פרידא's claim that always letting a כהן lead ברכת המזון was a merit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יוחנן rules that a תלמיד חכם who lets even an ignorant כהן גדול lead deserves death, because he lowers the honor of Torah. So letting a כהן lead looks like a serious wrong, not a virtue.

steps.title: He meant only a כהן who was his equal
steps.stepSummary: רבי פרידא's practice applied only when the כהן was as learned as he was. Then the honor of כהונה tips the balance, and Torah honor is not lowered.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he said this, he meant in a case where they were equal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 5. It explains that רבי פרידא only stepped aside for a כהן who was his equal in Torah learning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן condemned a תלמיד חכם who lets an ignorant כהן lead, because that lowers the honor of Torah. If the כהן is also a תלמיד חכם, Torah loses no honor. The extra honor of כהונה then makes it right to let him lead. So the two statements do not conflict, because they speak about different cases.

keyTerms.meaning: When he said (this). Used to limit what someone meant.
In (a case of) equals, meaning the כהן was equal to him in Torah

steps.whatToRemember: Honoring a כהן is good, but not at the cost of Torah honor. A תלמיד חכם should step aside only for a כהן who is his equal in learning.

phrases.english: When he said it, (he meant) in a case of equals.
phrases.notes: Equals in Torah knowledge. The כהן was also a תלמיד חכם.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָאָמַר אִיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 5 by narrowing the case of רבי פרידא's practice.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא). The practice applies only when both are equal in Torah.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed that רבי פרידא let any כהן lead, even an ignorant one, which רבי יוחנן condemned.
steps.terutzMaskana: He let only a כהן equal to him in Torah lead, so Torah honor was not lowered.

steps.title: רבי נחוניא בן הקנה lists his three merits for long life
steps.stepSummary: His students ask רבי נחוניא בן הקנה how he earned long life. He names three practices: he never gained honor through someone else's shame, he never went to bed with someone's curse on him, and he was generous with his money.
steps.simpleTranslation: His students asked רבי נחוניא בן הקנה: Through what (merit) did you live long? He said to them: In all my days, I never gained honor through my friend's shame. My friend's curse never went up with me onto my bed. And I was generous with my money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story in the series of sages who explained their long life. Here רבי נחוניא בן הקנה gives three practices, and the next steps explain them one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a fresh list, like רבי פרידא's list before it. All three practices are about how he treated other people. The גמרא will now explain each of the three in turn (steps 8, 9 and 10), because their exact meaning is not obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: In what (merit) did you live long?
I was honored / I gained honor
A generous person who easily gives up what is owed to him

steps.confusionAlert: "My friend's curse never went up on my bed" does not mean nobody ever cursed him. It means he never went to sleep while someone was still upset with him or while he still held a grudge. The next steps make this clear.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו אֶת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה:
phrases.english: His students asked Rabbi Nechunya ben HaKana:
Through what (merit) did you live long?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם: מִיָּמַי לֹא נִתְכַּבַּדְתִּי בִּקְלוֹן חֲבֵרִי,
phrases.english: He said to them: In all my days I never gained honor through my friend's shame,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל מִטָּתִי קִלְלַת חֲבֵרִי,
phrases.english: and my friend's curse never went up with me onto my bed,
and I was generous with my money.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו אֶת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the discussion of רבי פרידא and opens the next sage's list of merits.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Long life came through three practices: not gaining honor through another's shame, going to sleep with no grudges, and being generous with money.

steps.title: רב הונא refuses to let his student carry his hoe
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains "not gaining honor through my friend's shame" with a story. רב הונא would not let רב חנא בר חנילאי carry his hoe unless the student carried such things at home anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: "I never gained honor through my friend's shame": like the case of רב הונא, who was carrying a hoe on his shoulder. רב חנא בר חנילאי came and took it from him to carry it. רב הונא said to him: If you usually carry things like this in your own town, carry it. But if not, I do not want to be honored through your being lowered.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the first practice and illustrates it with a real story about רב הונא and his student.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The student wanted to honor his teacher by carrying the hoe. רב הונא saw that if this was beneath the student's normal dignity, his own honor would come from the student's embarrassment. So he allowed it only if carrying such tools was normal for the student. This shows what the practice looks like in daily life.

keyTerms.meaning: Like this case of... (introduces an example)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that true honor must not be built on another person's discomfort, even when that person offers the honor willingly.

phrases.english: "I never gained honor through my friend's shame":
phrases.notes: The גמרא quotes the first practice in order to explain it.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא דָּרֵי מָרָא אַכַּתְפֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: Like the case of Rav Huna, who was carrying a hoe on his shoulder.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתָא רַב חָנָא בַּר חֲנִילַאי וְקָא דָרֵי מִינֵּיהּ.
phrases.english: Rav Chana bar Chanilai came and took it from him to carry it.
phrases.notes: He did this out of respect for his teacher.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי רְגִילַתְּ דְּדָרֵית בְּמָאתָיךְ — דְּרִי,
phrases.english: He said to him: If you usually carry (such things) in your own town, carry it;

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי לָא, אִתְיַיקּוֹרֵי אֲנָא בְּזִילוּתָא דִּידָךְ לָא נִיחָא לִי.
phrases.english: but if not, being honored through your being lowered is not pleasing to me.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא נִתְכַּבַּדְתִּי בִּקְלוֹן חֲבֵרִי כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first of the three practices listed in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not accept honor that comes at the cost of someone else's dignity.

steps.title: מר זוטרא forgives everyone before sleeping
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains "my friend's curse never went up on my bed" through מר זוטרא. Every night before going to bed, he forgave anyone who had hurt him.
steps.simpleTranslation: "My friend's curse never went up with me onto my bed": like the case of מר זוטרא. When he went up to his bed, he would say: I forgive anyone who has hurt me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats the second practice and explains it with מר זוטרא's nightly habit of forgiving everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase does not mean that nobody ever upset him. It means he never went to sleep holding a grudge, so no one was punished because of him. The third practice, being generous with money, is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Who has hurt or pained me

steps.whatToRemember: רבי נחוניא בן הקנה's merits are about how he treated people. He refused honor that shamed others, and he never went to sleep holding a grudge.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל מִטָּתִי קִלְלַת חֲבֵרִי —
phrases.english: "And my friend's curse never went up with me onto my bed":
phrases.notes: The גמרא quotes the second practice in order to explain it.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּמַר זוּטְרָא כִּי הֲוָה סָלֵיק לְפוּרְיֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Like the case of Mar Zutra: when he would go up to his bed,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: שְׁרֵי לֵיהּ לְכׇל מַאן דְּצַעֲרָן.
phrases.english: he would say: I forgive anyone who has hurt me.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עָלְתָה עַל מִטָּתִי קִלְלַת חֲבֵרִי כִּי הָא דְּמַר זוּטְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second of the three practices listed in step 7, just as step 8 explained the first.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forgive everyone who hurt you before going to sleep.

steps.title: Being generous with money, like איוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבי נחוניא's third practice, being generous with money. It uses the example of איוב, who would leave his change with the shopkeeper.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And I was generous with my money." This means what the Master said: איוב was generous with his money, because he would leave a פרוטה of his money with the shopkeeper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the last of the three practices that רבי נחוניא בן הקנה listed: being generous with money. It gives איוב as the model.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In steps 8 and 9 the גמרא explained the first two practices with stories about רב הונא and מר זוטרא. Here it finishes the list. Being generous means not insisting on every last coin: איוב let the shopkeeper keep the small change instead of demanding it back.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone who gives in easily and does not insist on what is owed to him; generous
Job, the figure from the book of איוב

steps.whatToRemember: רבי נחוניא בן הקנה's three practices for long life: he never gained honor through someone else's shame, he never went to bed with anyone's curse on him, and he was generous with his money, like איוב leaving his change behind.

phrases.english: "And I was generous with my money"
phrases.notes: Quoting the third practice of רבי נחוניא בן הקנה

phrases.english: As the Master said:
Job was generous with his money,
for he would leave a peruta of his money with the shopkeeper.
phrases.notes: He did not demand his small change back

steps.triggerLanguage: וּוַתְּרָן בְּמָמוֹנִי הָיִיתִי — דְּאָמַר מָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the pattern of steps 8-9, explaining the third and last practice from step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Being generous with money means not insisting on small sums you are owed, like איוב leaving his change with the shopkeeper.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא asks רבי נחוניא הגדול about his long life
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא asks רבי נחוניא הגדול how he lived so long. The attendants beat him, so he climbs a palm tree and asks a Torah question. רבי נחוניא sees he is a scholar and tells them to leave him alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי עקיבא asked רבי נחוניא הגדול: "Through what did you live so long?" The attendants came and started hitting him. He climbed up and sat on top of a palm tree. He said to him: "My teacher, if the verse says 'lamb,' why does it also say 'one'?" רבי נחוניא said to the attendants: "He is a young Torah scholar. Leave him alone."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story about the same question, how did you earn long life. Two questions are now open, one about long life and one about the word 'one,' and the next two steps will answer them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attendants took the question as an insult, as if רבי עקיבא were saying 'why are you still alive?' רבי עקיבא then asks a sharp question about the קרבן תמיד: the word 'lamb' already means a single animal, so why add 'one'? The quality of this question proves he is a serious learner, and that is why he is spared.

keyTerms.meaning: Lamb (the animal for the daily קרבן תמיד)

steps.confusionAlert: The attendants were not hitting רבי עקיבא because the question was forbidden. They thought it was rude, as if he were asking why רבי נחוניא had not died yet. The Torah question was a separate question, and it showed he was a real scholar asking sincerely.

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאַל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אֶת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא הַגָּדוֹל
phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nechunya the Great
(he said to him): Through what did you live long?
The attendants came and were hitting him.
phrases.notes: They felt the question was disrespectful

phrases.english: He climbed up and sat on top of a palm tree.
He said to him: My teacher,
If it says "lamb," why does it say "one"?
phrases.notes: Referring to the verse about the daily offering (במדבר כח:ד)

phrases.english: He said to them: He is a young Torah scholar,
leave him alone.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אֶת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא הַגָּדוֹל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a parallel story with the same question that רבי נחוניא בן הקנה's students asked in step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sincere Torah question shows a person is a scholar and earns him respect.

steps.title: 'One' means the best of the flock
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחוניא answers the Torah question: 'one' means the lamb must be the finest in its flock.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: "'One' means the special one of its flock."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי נחוניא answers רבי עקיבא's Torah question first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'one' is not repeating the count. It teaches about quality: the lamb for the קרבן תמיד should be the choicest one in the flock.

keyTerms.meaning: The daily offering in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: He said to him: "One" —
the choicest of its flock.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״אֶחָד״ — מְיוּחָד שֶׁבְּעֶדְרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Torah question asked in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'One' teaches that the lamb must be the choicest of its flock.

steps.title: רבי נחוניא הגדול's three practices for long life
steps.stepSummary: רבי נחוניא answers the original question. He never took gifts, he never insisted on getting even with people who wronged him, and he was generous with his money.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: "All my days I never accepted gifts, I never insisted on paying people back for what they did to me, and I was generous with my money."
steps.whatsHappening: Now רבי נחוניא answers רבי עקיבא's first question about how he lived so long, and lists three practices.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two practices here are new: refusing gifts, and letting go of wrongs instead of settling scores. Not settling scores is close to מר זוטרא forgiving everyone each night in step 9. The third practice, being generous with money, is word for word the same as רבי נחוניא בן הקנה's practice explained in step 10.

keyTerms.meaning: I insisted on my measures; I demanded payback from people who wronged me

steps.whatToRemember: Long life is linked to character: not taking gifts, letting go of wrongs, and being generous with money.
steps.whyThisMatters: Both stories teach the same lesson: long life comes from humility, forgiving others, and generosity, not from anything dramatic.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מִיָּמַי לֹא קִבַּלְתִּי מַתָּנוֹת,
phrases.english: He said to him: In all my days I never accepted gifts,
and I never insisted on paying people back,
phrases.notes: He let go of wrongs done to him

phrases.english: and I was generous with my money.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מִיָּמַי לֹא קִבַּלְתִּי מַתָּנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the long-life question from step 11 and repeats the generosity practice from step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How רבי נחוניא הגדול earned long life
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: By never accepting gifts, never insisting on payback, and being generous with his money.

steps.title: Never taking gifts: the example of רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains 'I never took gifts' through רבי אלעזר. He refused both gifts and dinner invitations from the house of the נשיא, quoting 'one who hates gifts will live.'
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I never accepted gifts' means acting like רבי אלעזר. When the house of the נשיא sent him gifts, he did not take them. When they invited him, he did not go. He told them: 'Don't you want me to live? It is written: "One who hates gifts will live."'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the first practice רבי נחוניא listed, never taking gifts. It shows what this looks like through the behavior of רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר treated even a meal invitation as a kind of gift, so he turned down both. His source is a פסוק in משלי that promises life to someone who hates gifts. This connects directly to רבי נחוניא's long life.

keyTerms.meaning: the house of the נשיא (the head of the Jewish community)
one who hates gifts will live (משלי)

phrases.english: 'I never accepted gifts'
phrases.notes: Quoting רבי נחוניא's first practice

phrases.english: like this case of Rabbi Elazar:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲווֹ מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ מַתָּנוֹת מִבֵּי נְשִׂיאָה —
phrases.english: when they would send him gifts from the house of the Nasi,
he would not take them.
When they would invite him,
he would not go.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: לָא נִיחָא לְכוּ דְּאֶחְיֶה,
phrases.english: He said to them: Is it not pleasing to you that I should live?
As it is written: 'He that hates gifts shall live.'
phrases.notes: משלי טו:כז

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא קִבַּלְתִּי מַתָּנוֹת, כִּי הָא דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the first item of רבי נחוניא's answer from step 13
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Refusing gifts, even invitations, brings long life, as the פסוק says 'שונא מתנות יחיה'.

steps.title: רבי זירא: refused gifts but accepted invitations
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא also refused gifts from the house of the נשיא, but he did go when they invited him. His reason was that his presence honored them.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the house of the נשיא sent רבי זירא gifts, he did not take them. When they invited him, he went. He said: 'They are honored through me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second Sage who also refused gifts, but drew the line in a different place than רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא agreed that gifts should be refused. However, he held that attending a meal is not really taking a gift, because the hosts gain honor from having a Torah scholar at their table. So the visit is a favor he gives, not a gift he receives.
steps.confusionAlert: רבי זירא is not arguing that taking gifts is fine. He also refused gifts. He only disagrees about whether a dinner invitation counts as a gift.

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲווֹ מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ מִבֵּי נְשִׂיאָה —
phrases.english: when they would send him gifts from the house of the Nasi,
he would not take them.
When they would invite him, he would go.
He said: They are honored by me.
phrases.notes: So his visit is not considered taking a gift

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא כִּי הֲווֹ מְשַׁדְּרִי לֵיהּ מִבֵּי נְשִׂיאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with רבי אלעזר: same refusal of gifts, but a different view of invitations
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Accepting an invitation where the host is honored by your presence does not count as taking a gift.

steps.title: Not insisting on getting even: רבא's teaching
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains 'I never insisted on getting even' with רבא's teaching. Whoever lets go of what others did to him has all of his own sins let go by ה׳.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'I never insisted on getting even' matches what רבא said. Anyone who lets go of getting even has all his sins removed from him. As it says: 'He forgives sin and passes over wrongdoing.' Whose sin does He forgive? The sin of someone who passes over wrongs done to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי נחוניא's second practice, not insisting on getting even. It brings רבא's teaching to show the reward for this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא reads the פסוק in מיכה as cause and effect. ה׳ 'forgives sin' (נושא עון) for the person who 'passes over wrongdoing' (עובר על פשע) done to him. ה׳ treats you the way you treat others, which explains the long life.

keyTerms.meaning: I insisted on my measure, meaning I demanded to get even
one who lets go of getting even

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא has now explained two of רבי נחוניא הגדול's practices: never taking gifts (through רבי אלעזר and רבי זירא) and not insisting on getting even (through רבא's teaching). His third practice, being generous with money, uses the same words that were already explained for רבי נחוניא בן הקנה through איוב.

phrases.english: 'Nor did I insist on exacting my measure of retribution'
phrases.notes: Quoting רבי נחוניא's second practice

phrases.english: as Rava said:
Anyone who lets go of exacting retribution,
all his transgressions are removed from him,
as it is stated: 'He pardons iniquity and overlooks transgression.'
phrases.notes: מיכה ז:יח

phrases.english: For whom does He pardon iniquity?
For one who overlooks transgression done to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עָמַדְתִּי עַל מִדּוֹתַי, דְּאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the second item of רבי נחוניא's answer
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who lets go of getting even has his own sins forgiven, measure for measure.

steps.title: רבי asks רבי יהושע בן קרחה how he lived long
steps.stepSummary: רבי asks רבי יהושע בן קרחה what merit gave him long life. He replies, 'Are you tired of my life?' רבי answers that it is Torah and he needs to learn it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי asked רבי יהושע בן קרחה: 'Through what did you merit a long life?' He answered: 'Are you tired of my life?' רבי said to him: 'My teacher, it is Torah, and I need to learn it.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new story starts with the same question that was asked of רבי נחוניא. This step sets up the answer that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה first takes the question as rude, as if רבי wants him to die. רבי explains that he is asking in order to learn a Torah lesson, not to be disrespectful. This parallels רבי עקיבא's question to רבי נחוניא.

keyTerms.meaning: through what did you have a long life?
are you tired of my life?
it is Torah and I need to learn it

phrases.aramaic: שָׁאַל רַבִּי אֶת רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha:
In what merit did you live a long life?
He said to him: Are you weary of my life?
He said to him: My teacher, it is Torah,
and I need to learn it.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאַל רַבִּי אֶת רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קׇרְחָה: בַּמָּה הֶאֱרַכְתָּ יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story that parallels רבי עקיבא's question to רבי נחוניא
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What merit earned רבי יהושע בן קרחה his long life?

steps.title: He never looked at the face of a wicked person
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers that he never looked at a wicked person's face. רבי יוחנן says this is forbidden, learning it from אלישע's words to the wicked king יהורם.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'In all my days I never looked at the face of a wicked person.' As רבי יוחנן said: 'It is forbidden for a person to look at the face of a wicked person.' As it says: 'If not that I respect יהושפט king of יהודה, I would not look at you or see you.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן קרחה answers רבי's question. The גמרא supports his practice with a ruling of רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אלישע told the wicked king יהורם that he would not even look at him if not for the honor of the righteous king יהושפט. רבי יוחנן learns from this that looking at a wicked person's face is forbidden. Avoiding it was the merit that brought long life.

keyTerms.meaning: the face or image of a wicked person

steps.whyThisMatters: This step turns a personal good habit into an actual prohibition (אסור), based on a פסוק.

phrases.english: He said to him: In all my days I never gazed
at the likeness of a wicked man.
As Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is forbidden for a person to gaze
at the image of the likeness of a wicked man,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״לוּלֵא פְּנֵי יְהוֹשָׁפָט מֶלֶךְ יְהוּדָה אֲנִי נוֹשֵׂא
phrases.english: as it is stated: 'Were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat king of Judah,
phrases.notes: מלכים ב ג:יד, אלישע speaking to יהורם

phrases.english: I would not look toward you, nor see you.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: מִיָּמַי לֹא נִסְתַּכַּלְתִּי בִּדְמוּת אָדָם רָשָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question asked in step 17
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: He merited long life because he never looked at the face of a wicked person, which רבי יוחנן rules is forbidden.

steps.title: Looking at a wicked person dims the eyes
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says that one who looks at a wicked person's face has his eyes grow dim. This is what happened to יצחק, because he looked at עשו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: 'His eyes become dim.' As it says: 'When יצחק grew old, his eyes became too dim to see.' This happened because he looked at עשו the wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר adds to רבי יוחנן's rule by describing what happens to someone who does look at a wicked person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן gave the prohibition, and רבי אלעזר gives the damage it causes. He explains that יצחק's blindness in old age came from looking at עשו. This shows that even a great צדיק is affected by looking at a רשע.

keyTerms.meaning: his eyes were too dim to see (בראשית כז:א)

steps.whatToRemember: Not looking at a wicked person's face brings long life (רבי יהושע בן קרחה). Doing so is forbidden (רבי יוחנן) and can dim the eyes, as happened to יצחק with עשו (רבי אלעזר).

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said: His eyes become dim,
as it is stated: 'And it came to pass, when Isaac was old,
phrases.notes: בראשית כז:א

phrases.english: and his eyes were dim so that he could not see.'
This was because he gazed at the wicked Esau.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר: עֵינָיו כֵּהוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds the harmful result of looking at a wicked person to רבי יוחנן's prohibition
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Looking at a wicked person dims one's eyes, as happened to יצחק from looking at עשו.

steps.title: Was looking at עשו really what blinded יצחק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אלעזר. רבי יצחק teaches that אבימלך's curse on שרה was fulfilled in her son, through יצחק's blindness.
steps.simpleTranslation: But was that really the cause? Didn't רבי יצחק say: Never treat the curse of an ordinary person lightly. אבימלך cursed שרה, and it came true in her child. The פסוק says 'a covering of the eyes.' Don't read it as 'covering' (כסות). Read it as 'blindness of the eyes' (כסיית).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the claim from Step 19 that יצחק went blind because he looked at עשו. It points to a different teaching that gives another reason for the blindness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר said יצחק's eyes grew dim from looking at a wicked person. רבי יצחק reads 'כסות עינים' as 'כסיית עינים', meaning blindness, so אבימלך's words were really a curse. That curse came true in שרה's son יצחק, which seems to give a completely different cause for his blindness.

keyTerms.meaning: The curse of an ordinary person (not a great or righteous person)
A covering of the eyes (the plain reading of the פסוק)
Do not read it as (a way of reading a word differently to learn something new)

steps.confusionAlert: The curse did not make שרה herself blind. It came true in her offspring (בזרעה), meaning her son יצחק.

phrases.english: But did this cause it for him?
phrases.notes: Did looking at עשו cause יצחק's blindness?

phrases.english: But didn't Rabbi Yitzchak say:
Never let the curse of an ordinary person
be light in your eyes,
for Avimelech cursed Sarah,
and it was fulfilled in her offspring,
phrases.notes: In יצחק

phrases.english: as it is said:
"Behold, it is for you a covering of the eyes":
phrases.notes: בראשית כ:טז

phrases.english: Do not read it "covering,"
but rather "blindness of the eyes"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא גְּרַמָא לֵיהּ? וְהָאָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the cause that רבי אלעזר gave for יצחק's blindness in Step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אלעזר's claim that looking at עשו caused יצחק's blindness
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יצחק gives a different cause for the same blindness, which is אבימלך's curse. Two separate causes seem to contradict each other.

steps.title: Both causes worked together
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that both looking at עשו and אבימלך's curse together caused יצחק's blindness.
steps.simpleTranslation: This and that both caused it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. There is no contradiction, because both reasons played a part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two teachings do not compete with each other. Each one gave part of the cause, so both רבי אלעזר and רבי יצחק are correct.

phrases.english: This and that both caused it for him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from Step 20.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought only one cause could be true.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both the curse and looking at עשו together caused the blindness.

steps.title: רבא's verse forbidding looking at a wicked person
steps.stepSummary: רבא brings a different source for the prohibition against looking at a wicked person: 'שאת פני רשע לא טוב'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: We learn it from here: 'Lifting up the face of a wicked person is not good.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the prohibition from Step 18. רבא offers another פסוק as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 18, רבי יוחנן learned the prohibition from אלישע's words to the wicked king יהורם. רבא prefers a פסוק from משלי that says directly that 'raising the face' of a wicked person is not good. He reads this as looking at that person's face.

keyTerms.meaning: Raising (looking at) the face of a wicked person

phrases.english: Rava said: From here:
"It is not good to raise the face of the wicked."
phrases.notes: משלי יח:ה

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר, מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the prohibition in Step 18 and gives another source for it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to look at the face of a wicked person, as learned from משלי.

steps.title: A blessing to reach half of my days
steps.stepSummary: As רבי יהושע בן קרחה is about to die, רבי asks for a blessing. He blesses רבי to live half as long as he did.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he was about to leave this world, רבי said to him: 'רבי, bless me!' He answered: 'May it be ה׳'s will that you reach half of my days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of רבי and רבי יהושע בן קרחה continues. Now we hear the blessing he gave before he died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע בן קרחה lived a very long life, so even half of his years is a long life. Still, the blessing sounds strange, and this sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: At the time of his passing

phrases.english: At the time of his passing,
he (רבי) said to him: My teacher, bless me!
He said to him: May it be ה׳'s will
that you reach half of my days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the story of רבי and רבי יהושע בן קרחה from Steps 17 and 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע בן קרחה blesses רבי to live half as long as he did.

steps.title: Why not all of my days?
steps.stepSummary: רבי is surprised and asks why the blessing is not for a life as long as his teacher's.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not all of them?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי asks why the blessing is limited to half. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If his teacher's long life was so good, why not wish רבי the same full length? The question shows that the limit on the blessing was done on purpose.

keyTerms.meaning: And not to all of them?

phrases.english: And to all of them (your days), not?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְכוּלְּהוּ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the blessing given in Step 23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the blessing is only for half of the teacher's years

steps.title: Your sons need their chance to lead
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה explains that if רבי lived that long, his sons would never get the chance to become leaders.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Should those who come after you just herd animals?!
steps.whatsHappening: He answers רבי's question. A shorter life leaves room for רבי's children to rise to greatness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי was the נשיא, and his sons would take that role after him. If he lived extremely long, they would spend their whole lives without leading, as if they were just shepherds. The half-length blessing was given out of care for the next generation.

keyTerms.meaning: Those who come after you (your sons and successors)
Will they herd animals? (meaning, will they stay unimportant?)

steps.whatToRemember: The blessing for 'half my days' was not stingy. It protected the chance for רבי's sons to become leaders.

phrases.english: He said to him: Those who come after you —
shall they herd cattle?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 24.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A life as long as his teacher's would keep רבי's sons from ever taking over leadership.

steps.title: Two brothers who stayed away from wicked non-Jews
steps.stepSummary: אבוה בר איהי took pride in never looking at a wicked non-Jew. מנימן בר איהי took pride in never partnering with one.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבוה בר איהי and מנימן בר איהי: One said, 'May a blessing come to me, for I never looked at a non-Jew.' The other said, 'May a blessing come to me, for I never formed a partnership with a non-Jew.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings two more sages who each say what good deed brought them merit. Both are about keeping away from wicked people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These statements match the earlier theme of not looking at a wicked person. The first brother avoided even looking. The second went further in another direction and avoided any business partnership. According to the explanation, the non-Jew meant here is a wicked one.

keyTerms.meaning: May (a blessing) come to me (a way of mentioning one's merit)

steps.whatToRemember: This whole section teaches that staying away from wicked people, by not looking at them and not partnering with them, is a source of merit.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבוּהּ בַּר אִיהִי וּמִנְיָמִן בַּר אִיהִי,
phrases.english: Avuh bar Ihi and Minyamin bar Ihi,
one said: May a blessing come to me
for I never gazed at a (wicked) gentile,
and one said: May a blessing come to me
for I never made a partnership with a (wicked) gentile.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַד אָמַר: תֵּיתֵי לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more examples of sages whose merit came from keeping away from wicked people.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Not looking at a wicked person and not partnering with one are both causes of merit.

steps.title: רבי זירא's students ask how he merited long life
steps.stepSummary: The students of רבי זירא ask him what merit gave him a long life.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא's students asked him: In the merit of what did you live a long life?
steps.whatsHappening: Another story in the same pattern begins: students ask their רבי why he lived so long. This question sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same question was asked of other חכמים in this part of the daf. It shows that long life is seen as a reward for specific good habits. The question opens the door to a list of practical life lessons.

keyTerms.meaning: You lived long (literally: you lengthened days)

phrases.english: His students asked Rabbi Zeira:
In what merit did you live a long life?

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו אֶת רַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of stories about חכמים and their special habits (following אבוה בר איהי and מנימן בר איהי).
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which behaviors earned רבי זירא his long life.

steps.title: רבי זירא lists his lifelong habits
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא lists seven things he was always careful about: kindness at home, respect for greater scholars, honoring Torah, constant Torah and תפילין, respect for the בית המדרש, and sensitivity toward others.
steps.simpleTranslation: He told them: In all my days I never got angry inside my house. I never walked ahead of someone greater than me. I never thought about Torah in filthy alleys. I never walked four אמות without Torah and without תפילין. I never slept in the בית המדרש, not a real sleep and not a short nap. I never rejoiced when my friend stumbled. And I never called my friend by his insulting nickname. Some say the word is: by his nickname at all.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא answers his students with a list of habits he kept his whole life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list mixes three areas: peace at home, honor for Torah and its places, and caring about other people's feelings. The two versions at the end differ in strictness. One version says he avoided only insulting nicknames. The other says he avoided even friendly nicknames.

keyTerms.meaning: I was strict / I got angry
A real, set sleep and a short nap
His nickname (an insulting one, or any nickname, depending on the version)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי זירא's long life came from small, constant habits: no anger at home, honor for Torah and for greater scholars, and care for other people's dignity.

phrases.english: He said to them:
In all my days I never got angry inside my house,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא צָעַדְתִּי בִּפְנֵי מִי שֶׁגָּדוֹל מִמֶּנִּי,
phrases.english: and I never walked ahead of someone greater than me,
and I never thought about Torah in filthy alleyways,
and I never walked four cubits
without Torah and without tefillin,
and I never slept in the study hall,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שֵׁינַת קֶבַע וְלֹא שֵׁינַת עֲרַאי,
phrases.english: not a real sleep and not a short nap,
and I never rejoiced when my friend stumbled,
and I never called my friend by his insulting nickname,
phrases.notes: חֲנִיכָה here means a nickname that embarrasses.

phrases.english: And some say: by his nickname (even a friendly one).
phrases.notes: The second version is stricter: he avoided any nickname at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: מִיָּמַי לֹא הִקְפַּדְתִּי בְּתוֹךְ בֵּיתִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the students' question from step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A list of seven lifelong habits of holiness, respect, and sensitivity.

steps.title: משנה: a ruined synagogue still may not be used for ordinary things
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that even a destroyed בית הכנסת may not be used for eulogies, rope-making, trapping, drying fruit, or as a shortcut.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: And רבי יהודה also said: A בית הכנסת that was destroyed: one may not eulogize inside it, may not stretch out ropes inside it, may not spread traps inside it, may not spread out produce on its roof, and may not use it as a shortcut.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. רבי יהודה lists ordinary activities that stay forbidden in a בית הכנסת even after it has fallen into ruin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item is a practical use people might want for an empty building. Ropes need a long open space, a ruin is a natural place for traps, and its roof is good for drying fruit. The משנה says the ruin is still treated as holy, so these everyday uses are not allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה (the start of a new משנה)
A בית הכנסת that was destroyed
A shortcut path through a building

steps.confusionAlert: The הספד here means a private eulogy that uses the building for one person's needs. A eulogy for a great public figure is a different case, discussed in the גמרא.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: And Rabbi Yehuda further said:
A synagogue that was destroyed:
one may not eulogize inside it,
and one may not stretch out ropes inside it,
and one may not spread traps inside it,
and one may not spread out produce on its roof,
and one may not make it into a shortcut,

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ וְעוֹד אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the stories behind and opens a new משנה about the holiness of a בית הכנסת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A ruined בית הכנסת keeps its holiness, so ordinary uses of it remain forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the basis for the הלכה that the holiness of a בית הכנסת does not disappear when the building falls apart.

steps.title: Verse proof that holiness remains even in ruin
steps.stepSummary: The משנה proves its rule from the פסוק 'I will make your sanctuaries desolate': the places are still called 'sanctuaries' even when desolate.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And I will make your sanctuaries desolate.' This teaches that they keep their holiness even when they are desolate.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a פסוק as the source for the rule it just stated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה still calls the destroyed places 'your sanctuaries' (מקדשיכם) while describing them as desolate. That wording shows that the holiness stays in place after the destruction. This supports all the prohibitions in step 29.

keyTerms.meaning: Your sanctuaries (applied here to בתי כנסיות)

phrases.english: As it is said: 'And I will make your sanctuaries desolate':
phrases.notes: ויקרא כ״ו:ל״א

phrases.english: their holiness remains even when they are desolate.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וַהֲשִׁמּוֹתִי אֶת מִקְדְּשֵׁיכֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural source for the rule in step 29.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a ruined בית הכנסת keeps its holiness.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ויקרא כ״ו:ל״א, 'וַהֲשִׁמּוֹתִי אֶת מִקְדְּשֵׁיכֶם': the places are still called 'sanctuaries' while desolate.

steps.title: Grass growing in the ruin should not be pulled
steps.stepSummary: If grass grows in the ruined בית הכנסת, one should leave it, so people feel pain and are moved to rebuild.
steps.simpleTranslation: If grass grew up in it, one should not pull it out, because of the heartache it causes.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds one more rule about the ruined בית הכנסת: leave the grass that grows there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might expect that weeds in a holy place should be cleared out of respect. The משנה says the opposite. The grass is a painful sight, and that pain (עגמת נפש) pushes people to rebuild the בית הכנסת.
steps.confusionAlert: Leaving the grass is not disrespect for the holy place. It is done on purpose, so people see the ruin, feel sad, and want to rebuild.
steps.whatToRemember: A ruined בית הכנסת stays holy, so ordinary uses are forbidden. Even so, grass growing there is left alone, so the sad sight moves people to rebuild.

phrases.english: If grass grew up in it, one should not pull it out,
because of the heartache it causes.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָלוּ בּוֹ עֲשָׂבִים לֹא יִתְלוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a final rule about the same ruined בית הכנסת, one that seems unexpected.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Grass in a ruined בית הכנסת is left in place, so the pain of seeing it inspires people to rebuild.

steps.title: No light-headed behavior in a synagogue, so no eating or drinking
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one may not act with קלות ראש in a בית הכנסת. Its first examples are that one may not eat or drink there.
steps.simpleTranslation: The גמרא begins. The Rabbis taught: In synagogues, one may not behave in a light-headed, frivolous way. One may not eat in them, and one may not drink in them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion by quoting a ברייתא, a teaching of the Rabbis from the time of the משנה. It states a general rule, that a בית הכנסת must not be treated casually, and starts listing examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה dealt with a בית הכנסת that was destroyed. This ברייתא now deals with a standing, active בית הכנסת. It first gives a broad principle, no קלות ראש, and then shows what that means in practice: eating and drinking are everyday, casual activities, so they do not belong in a holy place. The list continues on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught.' This opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the era of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself.
Light-headedness, frivolity. Acting casually, without seriousness.
One may not conduct oneself, one may not act.

steps.confusionAlert: Eating and drinking are not forbidden because they are 'bad.' They are forbidden because doing ordinary daily activities in a holy place treats it like an ordinary place. That is what קלות ראש means here.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is the main source for the halachic rules of how to behave in a בית הכנסת. These rules are still followed today.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
phrases.notes: Marks the start of the גמרא's discussion of the משנה.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught (in a ברייתא):
Synagogues:
phrases.notes: The topic of the teaching.

phrases.english: one may not act inside them with light-headedness.
phrases.notes: This is the general principle. Everything that follows is an example of it.

phrases.english: One may not eat in them,
and one may not drink in them,
phrases.notes: The list continues in the next part of the ברייתא.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: בָּתֵּי כְנֵסִיּוֹת אֵין נוֹהֲגִין בָּהֶן קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The משנה (Step 29) dealt with a destroyed בית הכנסת. The גמרא now brings a ברייתא that sets out how to behave in a standing בית הכנסת. This broadens the topic from ruins to active synagogues.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a בית הכנסת one may not act with קלות ראש. Therefore eating and drinking there are forbidden. More examples follow.
